opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the biggest reason for optimism is that foundation models have shown us a recipe that actually works, and that recipe isn't specific to language. If you look at what happened with GPT-style models, the lesson was: take a very general architecture, feed it an enormous amount of diverse data, scale up compute, and you get capabilities that nobody explicitly programmed. Things like reasoning, in-context learning, following instructions. I don't see any fundamental reason that recipe should stop at text and pixels.

The second reason is more practical: we can stand on the shoulders of these models. A robot foundation model doesn't have to learn everything from scratch. Vision-language models already understand a lot about the world: what a cup is, that you hold it by the handle, that you shouldn't put it upside down when it's full. That common sense used to be the hardest part of robotics, and now we get a big chunk of it almost for free. What's left is the part that's uniquely robotic, the low-level motor control and physical interaction, the "System 1" reflexes, if you will.

And the third thing is the data problem, which has always been the bottleneck in robotics. Unlike language models, we can't just scrape the internet for motor control data, because it doesn't exist there. But foundation models are helping us here too. We can learn from internet video of humans doing things. We can use simulation, which is getting dramatically better thanks to GPUs, so we can run thousands of parallel worlds faster than real time. And now we have generative models that can produce synthetic data, essentially neural simulation. So I think of it as a data pyramid: internet-scale data at the bottom, simulation and synthetic data in the middle, and real robot teleoperation data at the top. Foundation models touch every layer of that pyramid.

Hardware is also catching up. Humanoids and other general-purpose robots are getting cheaper and more capable. So for the first time, the model side, the data side, and the hardware side are all maturing together. That convergence is why I think this is the moment, and why I believe a general-purpose robot brain is no longer a question of if, but when.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the simplest way to put it is that the hardest part of robotics turned out not to be the robot. For decades we were trying to hand-engineer perception, hand-engineer planning, hand-engineer control, and each of those pieces was brittle. What the foundation model wave showed us is that if you pick a sufficiently general architecture, feed it an enormous and diverse stream of data, and train it on a simple objective, you get capabilities that nobody explicitly programmed in. Language models learned to code, to reason step by step, to translate, all from next-token prediction. Vision models learned to segment and recognize things they'd never been labeled on. That recipe, scale plus generality, has now worked across enough modalities that I'd be surprised if the physical world were the one exception.

The second reason is that a lot of what a robot needs is already in these models. If you ask a large language model how to make a cup of coffee, it knows the steps, it knows that the mug goes under the spout and not next to it, it knows what "gently" means. If you ask a vision-language model what's on a cluttered table, it can tell you. That's common-sense world knowledge, and it used to be the hardest thing to get into a robot. Now we can inherit it. The robot foundation model doesn't start from zero; it starts from everything the internet taught these models about how the world works, and we're really just adding the last piece, which is grounding that knowledge in actions.

The third thing is tooling. The same infrastructure that made GPT possible, the GPUs, the distributed training stacks, the data pipelines, applies directly to robotics. And simulation has caught up. We can now generate millions of hours of physically plausible robot experience in simulation, use generative models to diversify the scenes and the tasks, and then transfer to real hardware. Data was always the bottleneck for robotics because you can't scrape the internet for joint torques. But between simulation, human video, and teleoperation, I think we're finally at the point where the data flywheel can start turning.

So when I look at the trajectory, I see the same early signals we saw in language around 2019 or 2020: models that are still clumsy, but that get noticeably better every time you scale data and compute, and that generalize to things they weren't trained on. That's the pattern that preceded the breakthrough everywhere else, and that's what makes me optimistic.

astra-6.text:
What makes me optimistic is that foundation models have shown us the power of learning across many different tasks with one model. In robotics, we’ve traditionally built systems for very specific tasks in very specific environments. That makes it hard to generalize. If you change the object, the lighting, or the robot, you often have to do a lot of work again.

A robot foundation model offers a different possibility: the experience you collect doing one task can help you do another. Language and vision models also give us a starting point. We don’t necessarily have to teach a robot every concept from scratch—it can build on representations learned from images, video, and text.

The big challenge is grounding that knowledge in action. Knowing what a cup is doesn’t mean you know how to grasp it, how much force to apply, or what to do when it slips. And we don’t have an internet’s worth of robot interaction data. So there’s still a substantial gap. But foundation models give us a compelling direction: build systems that can accumulate experience and transfer what they learn, instead of starting over for every task.

r003.rationale: It says foundation models learn across many tasks with one model and presents robot foundation models as able to transfer experience across tasks, conveying that generalizability as a basis for robotics.

r004.rationale: It discusses grounding knowledge in physical actions, but does not propose frontier models generating action tokens to control robots.

sol-6.1.text:
What makes me optimistic is that we’ve seen the same recipe work across very different domains: train a sufficiently large model on diverse data, and it starts to develop capabilities that generalize beyond any individual task. Language models are the clearest example, but we’re also seeing it in vision and video.

Robotics has traditionally been much more specialized. You build a system for one robot, one task, one environment, and changing any of those can require a lot of engineering. A robot foundation model offers a different possibility: a shared model that can learn across tasks, environments, and robot embodiments, then adapt to something new with relatively little additional data.

The big challenge is data. We have an enormous amount of text on the internet, but we don’t have an equivalent amount of robot experience. So I’m excited about combining sources: videos of people interacting with the world, demonstrations collected on real robots, and experience generated in simulation. Foundation models give us a way to bring those sources together.

That doesn’t mean language modeling alone solves robotics. A robot has to act in the physical world, where mistakes matter. But we now have strong evidence that general-purpose representations can emerge from learning at scale. That makes the idea of a general-purpose robot much more plausible.
